item.research_question: How do cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying methods, combined with vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C, affect the microstructure, hardness, and corrosive wear properties of CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings in simulated seawater drilling fluid?
item.material_system: CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy coatings on 35CrMo steel substrate
item.processing_route: Coatings prepared by cold spraying (CS) and high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying (HVOF) using hydrogen as fuel; followed by vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, 700 °C, and 900 °C for 2 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min in a vacuum of <10⁻⁴ Pa
item.test_conditions: Friction and wear tests conducted in simulated seawater drilling fluid using a Φ6 silicon nitride ball, 10 N normal load, 5 Hz frequency, 1800 s duration, and 6 mm stroke
key_findings: CoCrFeNiMn coatings prepared by CS and HVOF exhibit dense structures with porosity of approximately 1.1% and 1.4%, respectively, and bond well with the substrate.
Both CS and HVOF coatings achieve maximum microhardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C, with values of 487.6 HV0.1 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively.
The wear rate of the CS-500 °C coating is 0.2152 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹, which is about 4/5 (0.2651 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹) of the HVOF-500 °C coating.
Wear rates for both coating types at room temperature are very close, at 0.2952 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (CS) and 0.3016 mm³ m⁻¹ N⁻¹ (HVOF).
Heat treatment at 700 °C and 900 °C causes a decrease in microhardness and an increase in wear rates due to grain coarsening and the formation of soft phases.
The HVOF coating exhibits higher porosity and more obvious peeling compared to the CS coating due to its layered thermal spray structure.
The wear mechanisms identified include adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear, and oxidation wear, with CS being mainly abrasive and HVOF showing more oxidative and adhesive wear.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the peak hardness and lowest wear rate at 500 °C to the formation of a heterogeneous structure with nanotwins in recrystallized grains and high-density dislocations. At higher temperatures (700–900 °C), complete recrystallization leads to grain coarsening and the formation of soft FCC matrix and B2 precipitates, reducing yield stress and hardness. Oxidation wear in HVOF coatings is exacerbated by the growth, rupture, and periodic peeling of oxide layers at elevated temperatures.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the HVOF coating has higher porosity and a layered structure leading to more peeling compared to CS.
item.future_work: The authors do not explicitly propose future work in the provided text.
quotes: The two types of coatings achieve maximum hardness after vacuum heat treatment at 500 °C; the Vickers microhardness of CS-500 °C and HVOF-500 °C are 487.6 and 352.4 HV0.1, respectively.
The CS-500 °C coating has the lowest wear rate of 0.2152 mm3 m−1 N−1, about 4/5 (0.2651 mm3 m−1 N−1) of the HVOF-500 °C coating.
The wear mechanisms of the coatings before and after vacuum heat treatment are adhesive wear, abrasive wear, fatigue wear and oxidation wear.
